title: Position: Modular Memory is the Key to Continual Learning Agents
claim: A continually learning agent needs distinct modules, with a core model, working memory and long-term memory linked by retrieval, writing and consolidation.
layout: Single panel, three boxes left-to-right, colored arrows, dashed line splitting internal and external regimes
description: A single block diagram of a memory-centric agent. Three large rounded black-outlined boxes sit left to right: Long-Term Memory (facts, events, episodes), Working Memory (fetched memories, current interactions, reasoning traces, feedback) and Core Model (patterns, concepts, skills, reasoning capabilities). Working Memory and Core Model sit inside a light blue shaded region. Purple arrows between long-term and working memory are labeled Retrieve and Write. Red circular arrows between working memory and core model are labeled Process. A blue arrow arcs over the top from long-term memory to the core model, labeled as skill distillation. A green self-loop on long-term memory is labeled refinement, compression and graceful forgetting. Orange arrows connect the core model and working memory to an orange External World box at the bottom, labeled Incoming Signals and Response/Action. A dashed horizontal line with gray side labels separates the Internal Regime from the External Regime. Dashed note boxes at the lower left explain Retrieve and Write.
caption: An illustration of the role of memory in unlocking continual learning through the construction of distinct modules. The framework comprises (1) a core model for perception and reasoning, (2) a working memory module for temporarily storing information relevant to the current interaction round, and (3) a long-term memory module that accumulates extracted experiences, facts, and observations. Knowledge stored in long-term memory is selectively retrieved into working memory and consolidated into the core model, steadily improving its capabilities.
abstract: Foundation models have transformed machine learning through large-scale pretraining and increased test-time compute. Despite surpassing human performance in several domains, these models remain fundamentally limited in continuous operation, experience accumulation, and personalization, capabilities that are central to adaptive intelligence. While continual learning research has long targeted these goals, its historical focus on in-weight learning (IWL), i.e., updating a single model's parameters to absorb new knowledge, has rendered catastrophic forgetting a persistent challenge. Our position is that combining the strengths of In-Weight Learning (IWL) and the newly emerged capabilities of In-Context Learning (ICL) through the design of modular memory is the missing piece for continual adaptation at scale. We outline a conceptual framework for modular memory-centric architectures that leverage ICL for rapid adaptation and knowledge accumulation, and IWL for stable updates to model capabilities, charting a practical roadmap toward continually learning agents.
